articles.title: The Dangers of Getting Advice from the Internet
articles.summary: Melissa and Courtney discuss how to cultivate discernment when seeking advice online and recognize the danger of letting AI or influencers replace wise counsel from the body of Christ.
articles.summary_zh: Melissa和Courtney讨论了如何在网上寻求建议时培养洞察力，并认识到让人工智能或影响者取代基督身体的明智建议的危险。
articles.title_zh: 从互联网上获取建议的危险
articles.content:
Melissa and Courtney discuss how to cultivate discernment when seeking advice. They talk about how sometimes we think we need information when what we really need is relationship.
They discuss what kind of advice they like to get from the internet or ChatGPT, why they don’t recommend it for wisdom issues such as marriage and parenting, and why we shouldn’t let advice from AI or influencers replace wise counsel from the body of Christ.
Resource Mentioned:
Kitchen-Table Counseling Within Your Local Church
Related Resources:
Let’s Talk: Finding a Mentor and Being a Mentor
Want to Grow in Wisdom? You Need Gospel Friends.
Why AI Parenting Advice Falls Short
Don’t Treat AI as Your Pastor
Discussion Questions:
1. When you face a difficult decision or struggle, where do you typically turn for advice?
2. How do you discern whether online advice is helpful or unwise?
3. What makes advice offered within a personal relationship different from advice taken from an online blog or influencer or generated by AI?
4. How might repeated exposure to ideas about marriage, parenting, or relationships on social media influence our thinking without us being aware of it?
5. What do we lose when we turn to online sources for counsel instead of investing in relationships with people who know and love us?
6. Who in your life knows you well enough to speak honestly into your decisions and loves you enough to do so? How can you cultivate those kinds of relationships?
7. How would you like to grow in your ability to offer wise counsel to others?
articles.author: Courtney Doctor, Melissa Kruger

articles.title: Beware Making Mental Illness an Identity
articles.summary: ‘All in Your Head’ is a concrete and compelling remapping of mental health culture with impressive explanatory power.
articles.summary_zh: “All in Your Head”是对心理健康文化的具体而引人注目的重新映射，具有令人印象深刻的解释力。
articles.title_zh: 小心让精神疾病成为一种身份
articles.content:
In the years since he was involuntarily committed to a mental health institution for bipolar disorder, Frederik deBoer has wrestled with both profound gratitude for a system that saved his life and also palpable frustration that his experience of healing has become so rare.
All in Your Head: Illness as Identity, Trauma as Fashion, and the Desire to Be Disordered
is the latest broadside from one of the internet’s most heterodox thinkers and writers. As an “old school” Marxist best known for writing
The Cult of Smart
, deBoer takes aim at how the cultural drift within his own tribe is responsible for making mental health care so elusive for those who need it most: “The tendency to treat mental illness as an exciting adventure, the endless romanticization of lunacy in popular culture, is one of many aggravations I have nursed for years” (8).
The root of his aggravation—the treatment of mental illness and disability as an
identity to be celebrated
rather than a
disability that needs treatment
—isn’t all in his head. The use of talk therapy rose 47 percent between
2019
and
2024
. A 2025
LifeStance survey
found around 29 percent of U.S. adults have self-diagnosed their mental health condition after consuming online content, rising to 50 percent among Gen Z (versus 9 percent of boomers). Of the people who self-diagnose symptoms, almost a quarter (24 percent) “rarely” or “never” feel the need to take the next step to discuss them with a qualified clinician.
DeBoer argues that rather than reducing the stigma surrounding mental illness, the inordinate attention given to the mildly and dubiously afflicted is a dangerous distraction crowding out help for the severely ill. Accelerated by social media, this “gentrification of disability” has become a full-blown social contagion, compromising even the experts and institutions responsible for mental health care (153–54).
DeBoer is largely right, and the cultural shift he identifies has real-world implications both inside and outside the church. But the same ideological priors that so sharpen deBoer’s critique also suffer from two significant blind spots that, were they addressed, would make
All in Your Head
the more courageous, more constructive, and, therefore, more widely read manifesto we need.
General Bipartisan Ire
If you picked up
All in Your Head
to understand how modern therapy culture spread like wildfire across social media over the last several years, it’s not immediately obvious why deBoer starts his argument with an in-depth analysis of the anti-psychiatry movement’s influence in late 20th century politics and academia. But, if you can forgive me the pun, there’s a method to his madness.
After a blistering critique of “rightwing libertarian” policies that neglected mental illness, he cashes in on the subsequent trust he earns with left-leaning readers to launch a series of absolute haymakers toward “a species of thought that sometimes amounts to a kind of leftist pseudo-radicalism or a libertarian fantasy” (198) that drives the “destabilizing . . . move from mental illness as reality to mental illness as symbol” (8).
American individualism and anti-institutional bias aren’t new, but the painstakingly specific way deBoer traces their spread through the culture surrounding mental health and therapy is refreshing and instructive.
Our “apolitical romanticism of resistance to modern society” fuels two opposite errors: On the right, mental illness is sometimes seen as either imagined or a symptom of weak character. But on the left, the same romanticism often describes mental disability as more
en
abling than
dis
abling, as if neurodivergent minorities don’t need society’s help—society needs theirs.
Gentrification of Disability
DeBoer’s emphatic rejection of this predominantly progressive error— of “making a medical disorder an identity”—is the “overarching principle of [his] book” (165). This is never more clear in what he labels “the gentrification of disability,” where “diagnoses bec

articles.title: How a Former Prisoner in Iran Wants You to Pray for Christians in Chains
articles.summary: Pray not only for what God might do for Christian prisoners in Iran but for what God might do through them, for his glory.
articles.summary_zh: 不仅祈求神可以为伊朗的基督徒囚犯做些什么，而且祈求神可以通过他们为祂的荣耀做些什么。
articles.title_zh: 伊朗前囚犯如何希望你为被锁的基督徒祈祷
articles.content:
Not long ago, I had a surreal phone call with two young Christian men serving prison sentences in one of Iran’s hardest prisons. They’re there because they refuse to stop preaching about Jesus.
When I asked how I could pray for them, their answer wasn’t what you might expect.
“Pray that we would not be released until our job here is finished,” they said. They had led numerous fellow prisoners to faith. Now, their chief concern was to remain inside long enough to disciple them.
The call took me straight back to the five years I spent in prison for my faith. Now, these dear brothers (let’s call them Vahid and Reza) were behind bars, and I was outside. As we spoke, I pictured the wards and corridors, imagined the sounds and smells, and remembered how hard it was not to know how many years I would be there.
But it was also an encouraging call. Vahid and Reza were in high spirits, talking about Bible passages that were sustaining them and how the Lord was at work. They didn’t see themselves in a miserable, dark place. They saw themselves in a different mission field.
Their focus was the same as Paul’s in Colossians 4:3: “Pray also for us, that God may open to us a door for the word, to declare the mystery of Christ, on account of which I am in prison.” Paul’s request wasn’t for an open prison door but for an open door for the gospel.
Pray for Gospel Fruit
Vahid and Reza’s request resonated with me. I remember being unable to pray for my own release. I tried on a few occasions, but I couldn’t open my mouth to ask the Lord to release me. If I’m following Christ, I cannot choose the path. I cannot choose the location. I should follow him wherever he goes. And as I followed him to prison, he brought beautiful fruit.
They didn’t see themselves in a miserable, dark place. They saw themselves in a different mission field.
I think of one prisoner, a devout Muslim, who was wrongly accused of spying for Iran’s enemies. He was praying he would be released and was frustrated to get no answer. He approached me one day, saying, “Farshid, our God is dead. But I’ve heard yours is alive. Will you pray for me?” Fearing it might be a trap, I took him quietly aside and prayed briefly in the name of Jesus: “Lord, you know this man. Please hear his prayer.” The very next day, the man rushed over excitedly and gave me a huge hug. That morning, he had learned his name had been cleared. He was released two weeks later. Our God is indeed alive.
The Lord was also at work softening my parents’ hearts toward Christ during those years. I always say that even if only for the salvation of my parents, my time in prison was worth it. So, when you pray for persecuted believers, pray not only for what God might do
for
them but—as Vahid and Reza requested—for what God might do through them, for his glory. Pray for gospel fruit.
Pray for Comfort and Endurance
I don’t want to make prison sound easier than it was. The suffering was real. So pray also for comfort and endurance.
They beat me; they broke my toe. But the prolonged separation from my two children was the hardest burden to bear. The day I went to prison, my son was 2 years old and my daughter was 7. Missing their childhoods was an unspeakable loss.
Yet I know others who have suffered much more than I did. I think of a brother currently in prison who has been tortured. I think of a sister who was sexually assaulted when she was arrested. Even the apostle Paul was at times “so utterly burdened beyond [his] strength that [he] despaired of life itself.” And his request to the church was simple: “You also must help us by prayer” (2 Cor. 1:8, 11). Brothers and sisters like these need us to pray for them with love.
Whatever the situation, we can pray that God would grant the suffering believer comfort, peace, and endurance. The more specific the prayers, the better. articles.title: Best Practices from Evangelistically Effective Churches
articles.summary: While thousands of Americans are dechurching, some churches are baptizing many new members. Here’s how the country’s most evangelistically effective churches are sharing the gospel.
articles.summary_zh: 虽然成千上万的美国人正在脱离教会，但一些教会正在为许多新成员施洗。以下是这个国家最有效传福音的教会分享福音的方式。
articles.title_zh: 传福音有效教会的最佳实践
articles.content:
https://media.thegospelcoalition.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/23102213/effective-evangelism.mp3
In the summer of 2021, pastor Luke Peterson moved to Columbus, Ohio, to look for lost people.
To find them, he joined a gym. He started building friendships. And then he began asking those friends if they wanted to come over.
“Word started getting around—‘You’re not going to believe this, but Luke’s a pastor,’” he said. ‘It created some intrigue, and people started coming. I used to have a note in my phone of how many people came to our church because I went to CrossFit Grandview. It was up to like 60 or 70 before I stopped counting because it was impossible.”
Peterson’s good at evangelism, and his church is too—last year, they welcomed around 500 first-time visitors. When he preaches, he knows about half his audience is probably unchurched.
Pastor Luke Peterson (right) chats with Capital Church attendees / Courtesy of Capital Church Facebook
This is unusual in a country where
40 million
adults have stopped attending church over the last 30 years, and where
76 percent
of pastors said “fostering connections with unchurched people” is a need in their church.
Much has changed since the Billy Graham rallies of the ’60s, the door-knocking of the ’80s, and seeker-sensitive church billboards of the ’90s.
In the past, “you could randomly walk up to the person pumping gas next to you and say, ‘Do you know Jesus?’” said Perimeter Church pastor Jeff Norris. “Could that still work? Sure. But more and more, we tell people to invite neighbors into their home. The reality is that evangelism is much slower, and more relational, than it used to be.”
Today, people aren’t as likely to
read
the Bible,
think
it’s the Word of God, or
go to church
. But they’re also less hostile to Christianity than they were five years ago. And while they read the Bible less—especially in Gen Z—the trajectory is
moving up
.
“We’re not past ‘my truth, your truth,’” said Rob Warren, pastor of Doxa Church in Madison, Wisconsin. “But people aren’t as sure that their truth is actually true.”
These days, evangelistically effective churches are keeping evangelism front of mind in the way they preach, train, and encourage their congregations. They’re celebrating small wins. And they’re leading with a high view of Scripture, prayer, and God’s sovereignty.
“We’ve seen all of our ministries grow—from kids to youth to college ministry to Doxa Church as a whole,” Warren said. “It’s not just one demographic of people who are getting saved. God’s doing something.”
Times Have Changed
Thirty years ago, evangelical churches leaned on programs like Evangelism Explosion or Continuous Witness Training to deliver evangelistic focus and training, church leader Thom Rainer
said
. Those structured initiatives fit well in a culture that was more Christian and more institutionalized—it took an average of
20 church members
to reach one person for Christ per year.
Today, it takes 50, Rainer
said
. “Evangelism efficacy, evangelism effectiveness, has definitely diminished.”
That trend is likely to continue. As
social media
and
AI
fill our time and
increase
our social anxiety, even relational evangelism is growing more difficult.
As social media and AI fill our time and increase our social anxiety, even relational evangelism is growing more difficult.
“I’ve got a new couple that moved into my neighborhood a while ago, and I haven’t even seen them yet,” said Daniel Simmons, executive pastor of campuses and central discipleship at The Summit Church.
This means equipping the congregation is more challenging—and important—than ever before.
“Evangelism can be this thing that is so burdensome and guilt-driven,” said pastor Christian Gracia. He planted King’s City Church in Las Vegas in 2024 with around 80 people and has seen the church grow to more than 400.

articles.title: We Need to Know Our Reformed Roots
articles.summary: This volume is an invitation to rediscover that heritage and to find fresh encouragement in the faithfulness of God, who has sustained his church through the centuries.
articles.summary_zh: 这本书邀请我们重新发现这一遗产，并在神的信实中找到新的鼓励，神几个世纪以来一直支持他的教会。
articles.title_zh: 我们需要了解我们的改革根源
articles.content:
What does it mean to be Reformed? The label is used frequently but not always carefully. For some, it simply refers to a particular view of salvation. For others, it evokes a tradition, a culture, or even an aesthetic. Yet historically, to be Reformed has meant something much richer.
While no single sentence can capture the fullness of the Reformed tradition, at minimum it means three things: to be biblical, to be covenantal, and to be confessional. The authority of Scripture governs our theology, covenant theology provides Scripture’s redemptive framework, and the historic confessions summarize and safeguard the church’s doctrinal convictions. Remove any one of those pillars, and something essential to the Reformed tradition is lost.
With “Reformed” in its name, it’s hardly surprising that Reformed Theological Seminary has long sought to equip pastors and church members in all three areas. In recent years, members of its faculty have produced substantial volumes on the Old and New Testaments and on covenant theology.
Now, with
The Westminster Confession of Faith: A Comprehensive Commentary on Its History, Theology, and Application
, they turn their attention to the confessional foundation of the Reformed tradition. The result is a volume that seeks not only to explain what the confession teaches but also to demonstrate why confessional theology remains vital for the church today.
What Is the Westminster Confession of Faith?
The Westminster Confession of Faith
takes its name from the Westminster Assembly, a gathering of more than 100 ministers and theologians convened by the English Parliament in 1643 at a time of profound political and ecclesiastical upheaval. The assembly was tasked with recommending reforms to the doctrine, worship, government, and discipline of the Church of England.
After more than five years of careful biblical study and theological deliberation, the assembly produced the Westminster Confession of Faith along with the Larger and Shorter Catechisms. Together, these documents have served as the doctrinal foundation of Presbyterian churches throughout the world for nearly four centuries.
The assembly’s influence, however, extends far beyond Presbyterianism. The confession has helped shape the broader Reformed tradition, providing the framework for later confessional statements. As a result, its theological influence shaped generations of Congregationalists, Baptists, and other evangelical Christians. The editors of this volume rightly observe,
The confession is also ecumenical because it found wide acceptance among Congregationalists and Particular Baptists in the seventeenth century, as two different groups of theologians adapted the confession according to their theological convictions, producing the Savoy Declaration (1658) and the Second London Confession (1689). Thus the Westminster Confession is relevant to Presbyterians, Congregationalists, and Baptists. (xx)
Why Another Commentary?
The Westminster Confession has never lacked commentators. From the 17th century onward, pastors and theologians have written to explain its theology. Quality works by
A. A. Hodge
,
G. I. Williamson,
R. C. Sproul,
and more recently
Chad Van Dixhoorn
have each served the church well in different ways. So why do we need another commentary on the confession, and what makes this one useful?
The Westminster Confession has helped shape the broader Reformed tradition, providing the framework for later confessional statements.
First, this isn’t the work of a single author but a collaborative effort by scholars whose expertise spans several areas of theology. That breadth allows the volume to approach the confession from different perspectives while maintaining a clear unity of purpose. Each contributor brings particular expertise to the section he addresses, but the volume as a whole is concerned with helping readers understand the confession and its significance for the church.
Second, the commentary is consciously pastoral. Rath

articles.title: If the Church Did Its Job, Would the Parachurch Exist?
articles.summary: Do pregnancy centers, food pantries, or campus ministries exist because the church is failing to do her work?
articles.summary_zh: 是否存在怀孕中心、食品储藏室或校园事工，因为教会未能完成她的工作？
articles.title_zh: 如果教会做了它的工作，教堂会存在吗？
articles.content:
I’ve heard it said more than once: “If the church did its job, the parachurch wouldn’t have to exist.”
For instance, I was consulting with a local pastor who wanted to see the church serve people in poverty in his community. It was important to him that the
church
do it, not a nonprofit. Since he understood that God’s kingdom is bigger than his congregation, he wanted to engage multiple churches in the project.
I suggested he consider forming a council of pastors and collectively hiring a staff member to manage the operations of the combined program. He thought that could work well for his context. I’m not sure he was aware of the irony. I certainly was: We’d just reinvented a variant of the 501(c)(3) nonprofit that he so keenly wanted to avoid in the first place.
While the allergy to faith-based nonprofits was especially strong in his case, many people accept the premise at a basic level. In my experience, this sentiment is just as likely to come from someone who works in nonchurch ministry as from a pastor.
If we understand the church is the core institution created by Christ to advance the kingdom of heaven, has it failed so badly that we need an army of auxiliaries to prop it up?
Clarifying Terms and Roles
I answer that the parachurch doesn’t exist because the church has failed. It exists because God’s commands naturally generate institutions beyond family, church, and state. Proving that starts with clarifying terms.
The parachurch exists because God’s commands naturally generate institutions beyond family, church, and state.
“Church” has
more than one use
in Scripture. In some contexts, it describes the people of God universally (Matt. 16:15–18; Eph. 1:22–23; Col. 1:18). In others, it’s a local congregational institution with the parameters God has placed around its operation (1 Thess. 1:1; 1 Tim. 3:1–5; Philem. 1:2; James 5:14).
“Parachurch” typically refers to faith-based nonprofits who serve people in need or provide evangelistic and discipleship resources.
Certainly, as part of the universal church, all God’s people hold equal status in advancing God’s mission, whether they labor as nurses, students, pastors, or tentmakers (see Acts 18:1–3). Just as surely, all God’s people shouldn’t merely attend but be accountable to a local congregation that enables their spiritual formation.
When not assembled, God’s people are charged with many tasks—everything from stewarding creation to seeking justice for the oppressed. We can fulfill these tasks as individuals, but it often makes sense to create or join institutions dedicated to fulfilling them.
Which brings us to a crucial point: God ordained some institutions specifically, and some emerged organically from God’s commands.
Ordained or Emergent Institutions
The family, the local church, and the government are
ordained
institutions. The Bible gives each ordained institution some guidance but also leaves a lot open to interpretation.
While these ordained institutions are necessary for all people, they aren’t sufficient to fulfill God’s myriad commands to their fullest extent. Thus, some institutions emerge from the commands, rather than from a revealed institutional structure:
The command to work led to the formation of businesses.
The command to pass knowledge to subsequent generations led to the formation of schools.
The command to care for the sick caused
Christians to form
the first hospitals.
The command to care for the poor, widows, orphans, and strangers led to the
formation of charities
.
The command to make disciples of all nations led to mission boards, publishing houses, and Bible-translation ministries.
This ordained-emergent distinction parallels Abraham Kuyper’s “
sphere sovereignty
” in its recognition of institutions not explicitly outlined in Scripture. Many of these commands can be fulfilled to some lesser degree by the ordained institutions, but there are limitations. A family may work without forming a business, but they’ll never raise a skyscraper.
Most be

articles.title: Ministry Lessons from the Puritans (with Joel Beeke)
articles.summary: Joel Beeke joins Matt Smethurst and Ligon Duncan to explore what the Puritans can teach today’s pastors about prayer, preaching, personal holiness, shepherding souls, handling criticism, and persevering in ministry.
articles.summary_zh: 乔尔·比克（ Joel Beeke ）与马特·斯梅瑟斯特（ Matt Smethurst ）和利贡·邓肯（ Ligon Duncan ）一起探索清教徒可以教导今天的牧师关于祈祷、讲道、个人圣洁、牧养灵魂、处理批评和坚持传道。
articles.title_zh: 清教徒的教训（与Joel Beeke一起）
articles.content:
What can pastors today learn from the Puritans?
Matt Smethurst and Ligon Duncan welcome Joel Beeke to discuss the lasting wisdom of Puritan pastors and theologians. Drawing from decades of studying and teaching the Puritans, Beeke explains why they placed such a high priority on prayer, personal holiness, and applying Scripture to the hearts and lives of their congregations.

articles.title: On My Shelf: Life and Books with L. Michael Morales
articles.summary: L. Michael Morales talks about what’s on his bedside table, favorite fiction, favorite rereads, and more.
articles.summary_zh: L. Michael Morales谈论他床头柜上的东西、最喜欢的小说、最喜欢的重读等等。
articles.title_zh: 在我的架子上： L. Michael Morales的生活和书籍
articles.content:
On My Shelf
helps you get to know various writers through a behind-the-scenes glimpse into their lives as readers.
I asked L. Michael Morales—professor at Greenville Presbyterian Theological Seminary and author of
Exodus Old and New: A Biblical Theology of Redemption
—about what’s on his bedside table, his favorite fiction, the books he regularly revisits, and more.
What’s on your nightstand right now?
Malcolm Guite’s
Galahad and the Grail
. Myths of origin hold potential for shaping a society’s culture and character. I believe Guite, aside from writing good poetry and a national epic, is endeavoring to reawaken (or refound) England to her rich Christian heritage. This volume is the first of a projected
four-volume work
that may well represent the new definitive collection of Arthurian legends.
Writings of the Ramban
, translated and annotated by Charles B. Chavel. Nachmanides is my favorite medieval Jewish exegete and commentator, and these essays illumine his character and offer gleaming gems of insight. His essay on redemption, for example, gives a nuanced understanding of eschatology in the Hebrew Scriptures. He argues convincingly that the exile threatened in Leviticus relates to the Babylonian exile that occurred in Jeremiah’s day, whereas exile in Deuteronomy uses more eschatological language and seems to relate to the exile after the Second Temple’s destruction.
Another essay records his Disputation in Barcelona, when Nachmanides was forced by the Spanish government to engage in debate with a Jewish Christian convert. The disputation eventually led to his exile from Spain since, as one of the intellectual giants of his era, he acquitted himself overly well. (Christian readers will, for the most part, be disappointed with the representation of our faith by his opponent, but the disputation is helpful in that it offers insights into the sort of questions about the Messiah we should think about more deeply.)
What are your favorite fiction books?
Aside from literary classics, I enjoy mystery books, especially medieval mysteries, although it’s hard to find good ones. Ellis Peters’s
Brother Cadfael series
is good, although aimed for a younger audience (and so a bit tame). She had a beautifully poetic sense of providence and justice, which makes for satisfying conclusions.
I also appreciate the espionage genre, such as the early works of John le Carré, like
The Spy Who Came in from the Cold
,
A Small Town in Germany
, and
Tinker, Tailor, Soldier, Spy
. Perhaps less thoughtful but often more fun,
Alistair MacLean’s books
never fail to offer a little escape into adventure.
What biographies or autobiographies have most influenced you and why?
Iain H. Murray’s
two-volume biography
of D. Martyn Lloyd-Jones had a profound impact on me as a young, inexperienced pastor—my copies are filled with underlining and scribbled notes. This account of the Doctor’s life and ministry not only led me onto the paths of the Reformed faith, but demonstrated God’s blessings on a faithful minister’s diligent commitment to the ordinary means of grace, to prayer and preaching. Many of the problems and challenges facing the wider evangelical church when I was pastoring had their roots in the era of Lloyd-Jones’s ministry, so reading his biography offered much-needed biblical wisdom and the discernment of hindsight.
Augustine’s
Confessions
is also a treasured book—it’s so personal and honest, and displays the sure and gracious hand of God in one’s life.
Confessions
is also about Augustine’s mother, Monica, and how she persevered in prayer on his behalf; and about God’s faithfulness and goodness in answering her prayers so abundantly. Throughout the book, readers also get fascinating glimpses of life in the late fourth and early fifth centuries.
What are some books you regularly reread and why?
Aside from regular Bible reading, it’s a challenge to reread many books, since my research-reading stacks are always waiting. Classics and modern classics, however

articles.title: How Can I Find the Motivation to Use My Time Better at Work?
articles.summary: Let’s start by counting the cost.
articles.summary_zh: 让我们从计算成本开始。
articles.title_zh: 如何找到更好地利用工作时间的动力？
articles.content:
I work for a property management company that oversees retail space. I haven’t been doing this very long, but I’m finding that I’m not as productive as I’d like to be. Often, entertainment and fear of failure keep me from working. How can I get motivated to use my time better?
Given that we’re to submit to our earthly masters with sincere hearts as unto Christ (Eph. 6:5), our productivity at work isn’t ultimately about our advancement or our employer’s success—it’s about our gospel witness.
From before the fall, God ordained our work for keeping, cultivating, subduing, and exercising dominion over his creation. We’re still called to that today in any work to which we set our hand—including the property management of retail space. As believers, all work invites us to leverage our God-given talents and strength to bless and bring order to God’s creation in order to glorify him.
When alluring distractions or a fear of failure hinder our labor, we can turn to him who calls us for the truth that will rightly spur us on.
Distraction of Entertainment
When entertainment distracts us from working, we should start by counting the cost. If we’re spending work hours on entertainment and then have to finish our tasks in what should be our free time, what else is this keeping us from stewarding well? It may be infringing on our time for relationships, spiritual disciplines, or true rest.
On the other hand, if our working hours are fixed regardless of how on (or off) task we are, such as a job we clock in and out of with responsibilities only while we’re present, why are we willing to steal from our employer by accepting their payment without exchanging it for the labor we promised? Maybe we need to “cut off” what’s tempting us by blocking entertainment apps on our phone and computer during the workday (Matt. 5:30).
If we’re spending work hours on entertainment, what else is this keeping us from stewarding well?
Once we do, how might we instead faithfully devote that time to our employer’s good, even being willing to go a mile beyond what’s expected of us (v. 41)? Maybe we provide the talking points requested for a presentation—but also organize them into slides to save someone else from having to do so. Maybe we address the three issues our leader ask us to correct—but also address two more we discovered in the process.
Perhaps if we worked with this level of diligence and care, like Joseph with Potiphar, we’d be given increased responsibility and influence that could be leveraged for the kingdom. Those who can be trusted with little can also be trusted with much (Gen. 39:1–6; Luke 16:10). Certainly, God would be glorified as we work with all our heart as to the Lord and not to man (Col. 3:23).
Fear of Failure
When a fear of failure keeps us from working altogether, we can start by digging out the root of that fear.
Do you fear that your limitations and propensity to error will keep you from succeeding? Acknowledge that inaction guarantees you won’t succeed, but attempts to succeed in the work God has entrusted to you allow the opportunity for his power to be made perfect in your weakness (2 Cor. 12:9).
When you feel discouraged by your insufficiencies, trust God to provide the wisdom and strength necessary for the work to which he’s called you—by prayer (James 1:5), the edification of his Word, and your humble pursuit of correction and growth through helpful resources and the example of others.
Do you fear others’ judgment when you fail? Remember that your purpose is ultimately to please God, not man, and that there’s no condemnation for those in Christ (Rom. 8:1; Gal. 1:10). When you make a mistake or fall short of what’s expected of you, admit your error, seek understanding about what to do differently, and move forward with the humility and resolve that may make others respect you even more than they did before.
Trust God to provide the wisdom and strength necessary for the work to which he’s called you.

articles.title: Simon Says: Inconspicuous Evidence of Eyewitnesses in Mark
articles.summary: Several features indicate that the eyewitness accounts of Simon stand behind Mark’s Gospel.
articles.summary_zh: 有几个特征表明，西门的目击者叙述支持马可福音。
articles.title_zh: 西蒙说：马可福音中不明显的目击者证据
articles.content:
When I watch Jesus films, whether the current series
The Chosen
,
The Passion of the Christ
in the early 2000s
,
or even
Godspell
from the 1970s, I can’t help but ask,
Where did they get those stories?
Sometimes I can piece together bits from Matthew, Mark, Luke, or John. Occasionally I detect legendary material from church history or the apocryphal gospels. But at other times, my best guess is “They made it up,” and I ascribe the scene to creative liberty.
When we turn to the Gospel of Mark, which most scholars see as the first extant telling of the story of Jesus, we might also wonder,
Where did Mark get these stories?
Around the 1920s to ’50s, the fashionable scholarly answer was found in a field of study known as
form criticism
. This enterprise tried to tie different sayings and stories of Jesus back to an occasion within the early church that would have prompted their creation. Though the heyday of form criticism has passed, the legacy of seeing the Gospels as a “mixtape” of various ad hoc literary traditions can still be seen today.
In contrast to form criticism and the Jesus-film industry, the canonical Gospels are sourced in eye-witness testimony and were written within living memory of the events they describe. Perhaps no other scholar has written so persuasively on this subject as Richard Bauckham in his magisterial
Jesus and the Eyewitnesses
.
Indications of eye-witness testimony are peppered throughout Mark’s gospel. Here we will consider just a few, each revolving around the name “Simon.” These are more obscure than what normally make their way into works on apologetics, but their subtlety is a strength since they are not the kind of details one fabricates.
We will discover that inconspicuous indicators of eyewitnesses reveal what is happening behind the scenes more than front-and-center observations.
Evidence of Simon Peter
There are signs that Simon Peter has been a significant source for Mark’s Gospel, despite Mark not making a show of it. The church father Papias famously
stated
that Mark was Peter’s interpreter, who wrote down what he remembered from his preaching. Though many scholars doubt Papias here, Mark goes out of his way to emphasize Simon Peter. Several features indicate that Mark is particularly told from a Petrine perspective.
For example, his prominence verges on redundancy when he is introduced in 1:16: “Passing alongside the Sea of Galilee, [Jesus] saw Simon and Andrew the brother of Simon casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen.” This is part of what Bauckham calls a Peter inclusio, so that his testimony brackets the Gospel of Mark (see 16:7).
Later in the narrative, those “sick or oppressed by demons” are brought to Jesus in Capernaum (1:32), the summary after the climactic exorcism at the synagogue (vv. 21–28). But sandwiched in the middle is the healing of Simon’s mother-in-law (vv. 29–31).
Similarly, Mark writes of when the disciples look for Jesus, “Simon and those who were with him searched for him” (v. 36). Details like these betray a “Simon-centric” source. Bauckham argues that, with few exceptions, “Peter is actually present through a large proportion of the narrative from 1:16 to 14:72.”
Several features indicate that Mark is particularly told from a Petrine perspective.
An oddity in Mark’s grammatical style reinforces not just Simon Peter’s perspective but that of all the disciples: Mark uniquely favors using plural verbs to introduce singular ones. For example, Mark 11:12 reads, “On the following day, when
they
came from Bethany,
he
[Jesus] was hungry” (emphasis added). This provides the perspective of the group, as opposed to Matthew’s retelling: “In the morning, as he was returning to the city, he became hungry” (21:18). This literary device occurs 21 times in Mark’s narrative.
Evidence of Many Simons
The name “Simon” occurs 11 times in Mark. It most famously refers to Peter (1:16 [twice], 29, 30, 36; 3:16; 14:37), but it also refers to the other apostle, “Simon the Z

articles.title: Broken Bodies Make Beautiful Temples
articles.summary: We must view our foreign-feeling bodies as vessels through which God demonstrates his redeeming strength.
articles.summary_zh: 我们必须把外在的身体看作是神展示祂救赎力量的器皿。
articles.title_zh: 破碎的身体造就美丽的寺庙
articles.content:
The Lord’s ways are not our ways (Isa. 55:8–9). Do we take this seriously, or do we revert to “our ways” in desperate seasons when we wander from God to seek meaning?
I revisit this battle every time I look in the mirror at a quadriplegic body I desperately hope is
not
me.
“Our ways” tell me that the body is incidental to identity. It’s an enticing lie that exploits disorienting bodily experiences such as
disability
, sickness, gender dysphoria, or other bodily insecurities hindering people from seeing meaning in bodies that feel foreign.
I don’t see the nobility of God’s image or a temple worthy to house the divine when I’m being catheterized, bathed, or rolled in bed to prevent pressure sores. For others, disfiguration, tumors, or injury characterize bodies they can’t wait to “escape” at the second coming. For still others, their bodies contradict strong inward feelings telling them who they “really” are. Whatever the motivation, we tend to downplay bodily meaning when we feel it compromises our dignity.
But this is
autonomy’s
way, not the Lord’s way.
Scripture tells us there’s nothing undignified about weak, broken, dependent, or foreign-feeling bodies. The apostle Paul says our bodies (of all conditions) are
temples
of the Holy Spirit (1 Cor. 6:19). No higher calling exists for the physical than to serve as a temple to house its Creator.
Paul’s claim is a hard truth for those with bodily insecurities, because it means we must trade the disdain we feel toward our bodies for contentment—a difficult but worthy exchange.
‘Glory of the Immortal God’
Paul is well acquainted with bodily fragility and limitations, yet he doesn’t hesitate to make the body central to the identity of people he calls “more than conquerors through him who loved us” (Rom. 8:37).
For example, Paul observes in Romans 1:18–31 that the quintessential sin resulting from “exchang[ing] the truth about God for a lie” (v. 25) and “exchang[ing] the glory of the immortal God for images resembling mortal man” (v. 23) is
bodily
sin that distorts God’s “very good” design for the body (Gen. 1:31). Thus, the “glory of the immortal God” of which Paul speaks is, at least in part, our bodies, which God created as his image (vv. 26–27).
In Romans 6, Paul includes the body as part of the life Christ calls us to after “we have died with Christ” and subsequently “also live with him” (v. 8). He exhorts us to use our bodies “as instruments for righteousness” (vv. 12–13).
Paul makes no exception for those with bodily insecurities. The body God gave you is an instrument for righteousness, no matter how broken or “inauthentic” it may feel.
God’s Image, Not Ours
Scripture teaches that my bodily self, no matter how foreign it feels,
is me
. And, like the rest of me, it doesn’t “belong” to me for two reasons.
First, we’re not our own because the Lord makes his temples. Under the new covenant, “the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands” (Acts 7:48), and the “Lord of heaven . . . does not live in temples made by man” (17:24).
I did not make myself. The Lord “fearfully and wonderfully made” me; I am his “wonderful” work (Ps. 139:14) and “workmanship” (Eph. 2:10). He “formed my inward parts” and “knitted me together” (Ps. 139:13). Even brokenness, including disability, is the Lord’s wonderful work (Ex. 4:11; John 9:2–4).
Second, we’re not our own because the Lord purchased us, body and all. Paul tells us bluntly, “You were bought with a price” (1 Cor. 6:20). A very high price: the death of his Son.
My body is his, disability and all. Nothing about me is “mine” to do with as I please. My body is a temple for
the Lord
, not for me. He designed, constructed, and purposed it. “I” am no longer my own. Rather, my body is “meant . . . for the Lord, and the Lord for [my] body” (1 Cor. 6:13).
My body is his, disability and all. Nothing about me is ‘mine’ to do with as I please.
God has purposed my broken body
and purchased my identity at the great price of his Son’s death to proclaim h

articles.title: What My Grandparents Taught Me About Pastoral Ministry
articles.summary: You’re being prepared for the work the Lord has for you in ways you may not understand until you’re standing in a hospice living room.
articles.summary_zh: 你正准备好接受主为你所做的工作，直到你站在临终关怀的客厅里，你才会明白。
articles.title_zh: 关于牧灵事工，我的祖父母教会了我什么
articles.content:
When I was in high school, and early on during the summers in college, I spent my days working at a local pharmacy. I got a one-hour lunch break, and I ended up going almost every day to lunch at my favorite place: Granny and PawPaw’s house.
I don’t remember how it started. One day, I drove over on my lunch break, and after that, it became my routine. They wanted to see me, and I wanted to see them. Sitting at their table instead of alone at a restaurant was comfortable and unhurried. At the time, I didn’t think much about it. I was just eating lunch with my grandparents.
But looking back, I realize the Lord was doing more than I understood. Having now sat beside countless hospital beds and in living rooms with families walking through suffering, I can see how those lunches prepared me for ministry in ways I didn’t yet understand. My grandparents taught me how to slow down, listen, and simply be present with people.
PawPaw
When we ate, my grandfather talked mostly about his time serving in the Korean War, his years as an insurance agent for Liberty National, or fishing, which he loved almost as much as anything in the world.
Courtesy Jared Cornutt
Of the three topics, he talked about Korea the most. The war had ended decades earlier, but it hadn’t really ended for him. It shaped the rest of his life. PawPaw survived the war; he never escaped it. He talked around it in the way men of his generation often did when they carried wounds no one had given them language for.
They wanted to see me, and I wanted to see them. At the time, I didn’t think much about it. I was just eating lunch with my grandparents.
When I sat across from him at that table, I didn’t know what PTSD was. I just knew Korea was never far from his mind. Now I realize why. My PawPaw came home from the war during an era when PTSD wasn’t understood. Men like him were told to put the war behind them. They were expected to come home, go to work, raise a family, and move on.
Many did. But many, like my grandfather, carried the war with them for the rest of their lives. As a boy, I didn’t understand that. I just knew him first as my grandfather, and I knew he loved me. I’m thankful that’s how I got to know him.
Granny
My grandmother had an tenth-grade education. She grew up on a farm in a poverty she also never fully escaped. She never had much of a formal education, but I can tell you this: She knew the Lord, and the Lord knew her. If you heard her whole story, you might call her life a tragedy. But due to her remarkable faith, she wouldn’t describe it that way.
Courtesy Jared Cornutt
I can still see her sitting in that rocking chair when I’d come over, reading glasses on and her Bible open in her lap. She was eager to tell me what she’d read that morning. She loved God’s Word because she needed it and depended on it. Every time I left her house, she’d tell me the same thing: “I’m praying for you.” That meant more to me than any gift she could’ve ever given, because I knew she wasn’t just saying it.
She really was praying for me
.
I now know there was much about her life I didn’t understand. But what stayed with me was that my grandmother loved Jesus, loved his Word, and faithfully prayed for her grandson. The Lord didn’t answer every prayer she prayed the way she hoped. But I’ve often wondered how many of God’s kindnesses in my life came through Granny’s faithful prayers.
Ministry Now
I share all this because I recently sat in another living room. It was different, but it felt oddly familiar. As I left that room, it dawned on me almost immediately that I was equipped to minister there only because of those lunches years before.
Every time I left her house, she’d tell me the same thing: ‘I’m praying for you.’ That meant more to me than any gift she could’ve ever given.
I visited a member of my church, a woman in her 80s, who has leukemia. The infusions aren’t working. Neither are the other treatments. Her doctor has told her, in words kind but final, to go home and ma

articles.title: What You Should Know About the Hebrew Roots Movement
articles.summary: The Hebrew Roots Movement is a modern version of the New Testament Judaizers who were rebuked by Paul.
articles.summary_zh: 希伯来根源运动是新约犹太人被保罗斥责的现代版本。
articles.title_zh: 关于希伯来根源运动，你应该知道什么
articles.content:
The hiss of the cappuccino machine filled the coffee shop, forcing him to lean in and raise his voice. “Show me,” he said, “where Jesus or the apostles ever told Christians they no longer had to keep the law of Moses.” I remember realizing that, if I were honest, I wasn’t entirely sure how to answer that challenge. I knew Christians weren’t under that law, but where in the Bible would I go to explain why?
In the years since that initial encounter, I’ve had countless such conversations with Christians who have become involved in the growing restorationist movement most often known as Hebrew Roots. This movement teaches that Christians are obligated to keep the ceremonial law—especially the feast days, the dietary laws, and the seventh-day Sabbath.
For most Christians, it appears out of nowhere. A church member begins lobbying for the Old Testament dietary laws. A spouse begins denouncing Easter, believing Christians are required to keep Passover instead. A small-group leader starts recommending YouTube channels that teach Christians are sinning if they don’t observe
Shabbat
. Before you know it, long-held historical Christian beliefs about the gospel, the church, and the new covenant are being openly challenged.
These aren’t isolated stories. I regularly hear from pastors, leaders, and believers seeing Hebrew Roots theology sow confusion, strain relationships, and, in some cases, draw believers away from Christ’s sufficiency. They want to know what it actually teaches and why so many Christians are being drawn into it. And perhaps most importantly, how should pastors and church leaders respond?
Hebrew Roots Defined
To answer those questions, we must first understand what the Hebrew Roots Movement is—and what it isn’t.
Over the past few decades, many Christians have grown disillusioned with shallow expressions of Christianity and begun looking for something deeper and more ancient. That desire has led some to seek out more liturgical and traditional Christian denominations.
Others, however, are drawn to Torah-keeping communities, believing these groups more closely align with the beliefs and practices of the earliest Christians. But careful study of history shows that isn’t the case. Rather than uniting believers to ancient Christian practices, Hebrew Roots provides a highly diverse movement that emphasizes ongoing obedience to
portions of the Old Testament
.
Before you know it, long-held historical Christian beliefs about the gospel, the church, and the new covenant are being openly challenged.
The Hebrew Roots movement isn’t a monolithic organization. Most groups don’t even call themselves “Hebrew Roots,” preferring terms such as “Torah-observant,” “Torah-keepers,” or “Pronomian.” It’s a loose collection of teachers, ministries, and online communities that have emerged from mainstream Christianity and believe they’re recovering the “true faith” taught by Jesus and the apostles. The emphasis on recovering long-lost and hidden truths sometimes leads to highly individualistic interpretations among Hebrew Roots adherents.
Despite their diversity, these groups share one central theological conviction: New-covenant Christians are required to keep the old-covenant law, and not doing so is sinful. This errant theology is commonly known as Torahism.
Whereas the Torah (the first five books of the Old Testament) is a beautiful and
fundamental part
of the Christian faith, Torah
ism
is a dangerous misapplication of the old-covenant commands God gave to Israel. And if the theology sounds a little familiar, yes, this is a modern version of the beliefs taught by the New Testament Judaizers and rebuked by Paul in Galatians.
It’s important to distinguish between Hebrew Roots and Messianic Judaism. The two movements are sometimes conflated because they look similar on the surface, but there’s an important difference: Hebrew Roots teaches
Torahism
; Messianic Judaism doesn’t. I’m speaking in broad terms here, and beliefs can vary by group. But I’

articles.title: 7 Keys for Thriving in Lifelong Ministry
articles.summary: Learn long-term planning from Joseph, artful delegation from Jethro, lifelong consistency from Daniel, and aged wisdom from John.
articles.summary_zh: 从Joseph那里学习长期规划，从Jethro那里学习巧妙的代表团，从Daniel那里学习终身的一致性，从John那里学习年老的智慧。
articles.title_zh: 在终身事工中茁壮成长的7个关键
articles.content:
At the starting line of an Olympic race, nothing looks particularly dramatic. The athletes stand still. The crowd waits. The runners’ muscles are motionless. The track lies open. Then the signal sounds, and in a matter of seconds the race is over. To the spectator, it may seem almost natural: a brief flash of speed followed by applause. But those few seconds are never merely a few seconds. They’re the visible tip of years hidden from public view.
Behind that moment lie thousands of hours of training. Victory isn’t won merely by speed on race day; it’s won through long obedience before the race ever begins. If you’re a believer, you’re in a daunting spiritual race with eternal consequences.
How much truer is this of the pastor, who also has the weighty task of shepherding other believers? If we want to avoid the all-too-common pitfalls of burnout, scandal, and disillusionment, we must follow seven keys to pastoral perseverance rooted in Scripture and biblical wisdom.
Key #1: Radically Trust the Holy Spirit
If we’re prone to neglect one person of the Trinity, it’s probably the Holy Spirit. This is a tragedy. If we can’t draw one breath of oxygen into our lungs without his aid (Ps. 104:29–30), how much less can we persevere in the ministry without his constant breathing of empowerment (John 20:22)?
I wonder if one of the reasons for a high dropout rate among pastors is that we often try to do the Lord’s work without seeking his rejuvenating power. This divine power comes only through ardent faith and prayer.
Oh, how we need conscious, wholehearted dependence on the Spirit! Those who sit under our ministry and preaching will be as dead as dry bones unless the sovereign Spirit breathes on them and transforms them into a mighty spiritual army (Ezek. 37:1–14; Eph. 2:1).
Key #2: Pray Like Your Life Depends on It
Prayer is the breath of the Christian and the heartbeat of persevering ministry. If you want to persevere, dear pastor, take every aspect of your ministry to the Lord in prayer—every sermon you preach, every class you teach, and every visit you make. Pray, pray, pray your way through the ministry!
Oh, what sweetness you’ll find in sacred, childlike dependence on your heavenly Father. As John Calvin
puts it
, in prayer we climb into the lap of our heavenly Father and whisper our needs in his ear.
Prayer is the breath of the Christian and the heartbeat of persevering ministry.
As ministers, we must be much on our knees in prayer. Our method of study should be on our knees, then back to our books, then back to our knees again. We never do our theology alone; we do so in the presence of the triune God. Perhaps we don’t cry out to God more in secret—begging for his help in holy desperation and importunity—because we often don’t recognize how weak and needy we truly are.
Key #3: Soak Up the Bible as Your Highest Calling
As pastors, our power in public depends in large part on the quality and quantity of time we spend with God in secret (Matt. 6:6). We abide in Christ in proportion to the degree that his Word abides in us, and the Word abides in us in proportion to how much quality time we spend absorbing it—reading it, meditating on it, praying over it, memorizing it, internalizing it, preaching and teaching it, speaking it, trusting it, applying it, and fleshing it out through practical obedience.
With the Spirit’s help, digest God’s Word with consistency, read it systematically, and absorb it experientially. Linger over every divine word. Bask every day in God’s presence. Cultivate holy familiarity with him. As you do so, your soul will be invigorated with life, strength, and vitality.
By marinating in Scripture as pastors, we can walk with God like Enoch (Gen. 5:24), cultivate friendship with him like Abraham (James 2:23), know him face-to-face like Moses (Ex. 33:11), and enjoy sweet intimacy with him like the psalmist (Ps. 25:14). Through the Word, we can savor God’s presence and gaze on his beauty (27:4).
As you soak in the Wor

articles.title: God Knows Your Name
articles.summary: One particularly catchy book promotion featured the auctioning of the chance for readers to have their name in print. articles.title: God’s Portrait of You
articles.summary: The British TV reality show Portrait Artist of the Year pits nine amateur painters against each other in creating portraits of a local celebrity. The images have to be completed in just four hours, which is condensed into the one-hour program. It’s fascinating to watch the cameras capture each artist’s creation slowly emerging from a blank canvas.
articles.summary_zh: 这位英国电视真人秀年度肖像艺术家让九位业余画家互相对立，为当地名人创作肖像。这些图像必须在短短四个小时内完成，并浓缩成一小时的节目。观看相机捕捉每位艺术家从空白画布上慢慢浮现的创作，令人着迷。

Moore said he wanted to paint them “in a position of power.” And that’s exactly what he did.

articles.title: Carried Through
articles.summary: Lillie Cunningham is 110 years old, yet she isn’t reliant on a cane or walker. She does rely on Scripture, however, which she reads every morning and night—and attends church every Sunday. When she considers her life, she states, “I just always had faith and trust in God that he was going to carry us through.”
articles.summary_zh: Lillie Cunningham已经110岁了，但她并不依赖拐杖或助行器。然而，她确实依靠每天早上和晚上读的经文，并且每个星期天都去教堂。当她考虑自己的生活时，她说： “我一直对上帝有信心和信任，相信他会带领我们度过难关。”

articles.title: In Step with God
articles.summary: Can you imagine sprinting as hard as you can possibly run . . . without being able to see? That’s what happens in Paralympic guide running. Blind runners compete with a guide, someone who runs alongside them step by step, connected by a short tether.
articles.summary_zh: 你能想象在看不到的情况下尽你所能地跑步吗？这就是残奥会向导跑步的方式。盲人跑步者与向导竞争，向导通过短绳一步一步地与他们并肩奔跑。
articles.title_zh: 与神同步

articles.title: Grace in Grief
articles.summary: The world watched the news in horror as the sightseeing helicopter flying over the river tore into pieces. As the main rotor and tail broke off, the cabin plunged into the waters below, with the pilot and a family of five trapped inside. Just days after the tragedy that had taken the lives of his sister, brother-in-law, niece, and two nephews, the brother was at the site honoring his loved ones.
articles.summary_zh: 世界惊恐地看着这条消息，观光直升机飞过河面撕成碎片。随着主旋翼和尾翼脱落，机舱陷入了下面的水域，飞行员和一个五口之家被困在里面。在夺走他姐姐、姐夫、侄女和两个侄子生命的悲剧发生几天后，这位兄弟就在现场纪念他的亲人。

articles.title: You Do It to Me
articles.summary: In September 1963, Welsh artist John Petts heard the news that a racially motivated bombing of 16th Street Baptist Church in Birmingham, Alabama, had killed four African American girls. Wanting to help, he offered to replace the church’s shattered stained-glass window. The people of Wales soon raised the funds.
articles.summary_zh: 1963年9月，威尔士艺术家约翰·佩茨（ John Petts ）听说阿拉巴马州伯明翰第16街浸信会教堂的种族动机爆炸事件造成四名非洲裔美国女孩死亡。他想帮忙，提出更换教堂破碎的彩色玻璃窗。威尔士人民很快就筹集到了资金。

articles.title: The Lesson in the Ruins
articles.summary: “You have to be careful about the snakes, insects, jaguars and everything else,” said archaeologist Ivan Šprajc. Wielding chainsaws and machetes, he and his team slashed through thick jungle to try to reach the lost city of Ocumtún.
articles.summary_zh: 考古学家Ivan Šprajc说： “你必须小心蛇、昆虫、美洲虎和其他一切。”他和他的团队挥舞着电锯和大砍刀，穿过茂密的丛林，试图到达失落的城市奥库姆通。

articles.title: Get Going with God
articles.summary: It was raining, bringing the temperature down even more. We were on a multiday hike in Nepal, and leaving the warm mountain lodge to venture into the freezing weather was getting harder each morning. “Let’s go,”
articles.summary_zh: 下雨了，温度更低了。我们在尼泊尔进行了多日徒步旅行，每天早上离开温暖的山间小屋冒险进入寒冷的天气变得越来越困难。“走吧。”

articles.title: Fishers of Sheep
articles.summary: It was one of those videos that makes you stop and do a double take—Yemeni fishermen frantically rescuing hundreds of sheep from the Red Sea. A ship carrying thousands of sheep had run aground off the coast of Ras Al-Ara, Yemen. The vessel was headed for Djibouti when it capsized, leading to the drowning of more than 160 sheep.
articles.summary_zh: 这是一段让你停下来拍摄双重拍摄的视频之一--也门渔民疯狂地从红海中救出数百只羊。一艘载有数千只羊的船在也门Ras Al-Ara海岸搁浅。这艘船在吉布提倾覆时驶向吉布提，导致160多只羊溺水身亡。
